docs.title: Fusion Engine
docs.text:
Fusion Engine is a 2D game engine built specifically for creating reinforcement learning (RL) training environments, scripted entirely in Python. Its component model is inspired by Unity and its nested-scene model by Godot, but unlike either of those, the engine's whole purpose is producing lightweight, fast-stepping environments to train RL agents in — not shipping games.

Platform support

Fusion Engine currently only runs on Windows. There is no macOS or Linux support at this time.

This site covers the Python scripting API — the surface you write scripts against. For the engine's internal architecture (the rendering pipeline, the three physics solvers, the ECS, the editor, and the export pipeline) see the design document (PDF).

docs.title: Where to start
docs.text:
• New to Fusion? Start with Getting Started — install the engine, create a project, and attach your first script.
  • Writing scripts? See the Scripting Guide for the full Python API: components, exports, physics, input, and RL agents.
  • Looking up a class or function? Jump into the API Reference.

docs.title: How the engine fits together
docs.text:
System Responsibility Rendering Engine OpenGL-based rasterization renderer Physics Engine Rigid body (PGS), soft body (XPBD), and fluid (PBF) simulation, unified through a shared impulse-based coupling layer Object and Component Manager Manages entities and their components (ECS) Editor ImGui-based editor UI, windows, and gizmos File and Project Manager Project/scene serialization, resource paths (res://), and export Script Manager The C++ ↔ Python bridge (pybind11) and script lifecycle

Reinforcement learning support (the fusion.RL module, the AgentComponent, headless training, and the training monitor) is an optional package, not part of the base engine — you enable it from the project configuration screen, and it's what pulls in Gymnasium, Stable-Baselines3, NumPy, and PyTorch into your project's virtual environment.

docs.title: Quick example
docs.text:
Every Fusion script starts with from fusion import *, so the engine's classes and functions (Script, Vector3, export, component types, and so on) are available unqualified:

from fusion import *


class Enemy(Script):
    speed = export(3.0)

    def OnStart(self):
        self.transform = self.get_component(TransformComponent)

    def Process(self, delta):
        self.transform.world_position += Vector3(self.speed * delta, 0, 0)

speed here is an exported property — export(3.0) makes it show up as an editable field in the inspector, defaulting to 3.0, while still working as a normal Python attribute in code. See Exporting properties for the full set of export widgets (ranges, drag fields, color pickers, file pickers, and collapsible sections).

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Windows. Fusion Engine currently only supports Windows — there's no macOS or Linux build.
  • Visual Studio, but only if you're building from source. The project is maintained as a Visual Studio solution and isn't currently set up for other IDEs or build systems.
  • Python 3.11 is the version the engine's virtual environments are built against. Later 3.x versions are also expected to work, but 3.11 is the tested baseline.

docs.title: Installing the engine
docs.text: You have two options: grab a compiled build, or build the engine yourself.

docs.title: Option 1 — Official release (recommended)
docs.text:
1. Go to the Releases page.
  2. Download the latest .zip archive.
  3. Extract it to a folder of your choice.
  4. Run FusionApp.exe to launch the editor.

No additional build tools are required for this path.

docs.title: Option 2 — Build from source
docs.text:
1. Clone the repository:
git clone https://github.com/DevPhusion/FusionEngine.git
  1. Open the cloned folder in Visual Studio.
  2. Build the solution.
  3. Run the resulting executable to launch the editor.

docs.title: Creating a project
docs.text:
When you create a new Fusion project, the editor sets up a few things for you alongside your resources folder:

  • A Python virtual environment, scoped to that project.
  • A compiled Python module (.pyd) that links the C++ engine core into that venv as the fusion package (plus fusionRL/fusion_gym if the RL package is enabled — see below).
  • A .pyi stub file, generated via pybind-stubgen, written into a typings/ folder in your project.
  • VS Code settings, written automatically, that point VS Code's interpreter and stub path at that venv and typings/ folder — so autocomplete and syntax highlighting for the entire engine API work out of the box in any script you open.

Two file types make up a project on disk:

Extension Description .fusion Project save file — settings and the main scene path .fscene A serialized scene — its objects and components

Resources (scripts, scenes, textures, etc.) are referenced internally using res:// virtual paths rather than absolute filesystem paths, so a project stays portable across machines. File.virtual_to_absolute() and File.absolute_to_virtual() convert between the two when a script needs a real path — see the Scripting Guide.

docs.title: Installing extra Python packages
docs.text: Because each project gets its own venv, you can pip install whatever you need directly into it — NumPy, PyTorch, or anything else your scripts import — the same way you would for any other Python project.

docs.title: Enabling reinforcement learning
docs.text:
RL support ships as an installable package rather than being baked into the base engine. Turning it on from the project configuration screen does two things:

  • Pulls the required Python libraries (NumPy, PyTorch, Gymnasium, Stable-Baselines3) into the project's venv.
  • Exposes the engine-side fusion.RL API (AgentComponent, fusion.RL.Environment) and adds the training-related editor windows (the headless training monitor and live-view toggle).

Installed/selected packages are synced automatically in the background whenever you open the project, so you generally don't need to manage this by hand after the initial toggle.

docs.title: Your first script
docs.text:
1. Right-click in the resource browser and choose New Script.
  2. Attach it to an object as a component (drag it onto the object, or use the inspector's "Add Component" and pick the script).
  3. Double-click it to open it in your editor — with the typings/ stub in place, you get full autocomplete against the real engine API.

Every script is a class inheriting from Script, and every script starts with a wildcard import from the fusion package:

from fusion import *


class Mover(Script):
    speed = export(3.0)

    def OnStart(self):
        self.transform = self.get_component(TransformComponent)

    def Process(self, delta):
        self.transform.world_position += Vector3(self.speed * delta, 0, 0)

A couple of things worth knowing right away:

  • Lifecycle. When an object (and its scripts) enters the scene, the engine runs a load pass over the new objects followed by a start pass — OnStart(self) runs once, during the start pass. Process(self, delta) then runs once per frame, with delta being the elapsed time in seconds.
  • Auto-registration. You don't need to manually register Mover as a component type anywhere. The first time it's used with get_component()/add_component()/has_component() (including the Mover(...) you attach in the editor), the engine registers it against its res:// file path automatically.
  • Exports. speed = export(3.0) is both a normal Python class attribute and an inspector field — see Exporting properties for the full set of export widgets.

From here, the Scripting Guide covers components, physics, input, and (if you've enabled it) the RL agent API in detail.

docs.title: Scripting Guide
docs.text:
Scripts are how you make things happen in your game: moving a player, reacting to a key press, spawning enemies. In this guide you'll write your first script, attach it to an object, and build a simple movement system.

By the end you'll know how to:

  • Create a script and attach it to an object
  • Run code when the object starts and on every frame
  • Print messages to the Console
  • Read keyboard input
  • Move an object around the scene
  • Expose values to the inspector so you can tweak them without touching code

Python

Scripts are written in Python. If you've never used Python before, you can still follow along. Every example is short and explained.

docs.title: 1. Creating your first script
docs.text:
Create a new script file in your project (for example res://scripts/player.py) and open it in your editor.

Every script follows the same pattern:

from fusion import *


class Player(Script):
    def OnStart(self):
        Console.Print("Hello from Player!")

    def Process(self, delta):
        pass

Let's break that down.

from fusion import * This line goes at the top of every script. It makes everything the engine provides (Script, Vector3, Input, Console, and more) available in your file.

class Player(Script) Every script is a class that inherits from Script. The class name is up to you.

OnStart(self) Runs once, when the object is added to the scene. Use it for setup.

Process(self, delta) Runs every frame. delta is the time in seconds since the previous frame. Use it for anything that changes over time, like movement.

docs.title: 2. Attaching a script to an object
docs.text:
A script does nothing until it's attached to an object in your scene.

  1. Select the object you want to control in the scene.
  2. In the inspector, add your script to it.

Press Play. You should see Hello from Player! appear in the Console window.

Tip

If nothing shows up, check that the script is attached to an object that's actually in the scene, and that the class name inside the file matches what you expect.

docs.title: 3. Printing to the Console
docs.text:
The Console is the easiest way to see what your script is doing.

Console.Print("Everything is fine")
Console.PrintWarning("Something looks off")
Console.PrintError("Something broke")

Each message is tagged as Info, Warning, or Error in the editor's Console window. You can also use f-strings to print values:

Console.Print(f"Delta time: {delta}")

docs.title: 4. Accessing the object's components
docs.text:
Objects are built from components. Each one gives the object a capability:

Component What it does TransformComponent Position, rotation and size RenderComponent How the object looks (color, shape, texture) RigidBodyComponent Physics movement (velocity, forces, mass) CollisionComponent Collision shapes and collision events

From inside a script, use get_component to fetch a component from the object the script is attached to:

class Player(Script):
    def OnStart(self):
        self.transform = self.get_component(TransformComponent)
        self.render = self.get_component(RenderComponent)

Storing the result on self (like self.transform) lets you reuse it in Process without looking it up every frame.

You can also check whether a component exists, and add one if it doesn't:

if not self.has_component(RigidBodyComponent):
    self.add_component(RigidBodyComponent)

And self.owner gives you the object the script is attached to:

Console.Print(f"I am attached to {self.owner.name}")

docs.title: 5. Changing things from a script
docs.text:
Once you have a component, you can read and change its properties.

class Player(Script):
    def OnStart(self):
        self.transform = self.get_component(TransformComponent)
        self.render = self.get_component(RenderComponent)

        # Move the object to a position
        self.transform.world_position = Vector3(2, 0, 0)

        # Make it twice as big
        self.transform.size = Vector3(2, 2, 1)

        # Tint it red (red, green, blue, alpha)
        self.render.color = Vector4(1, 0, 0, 1)

docs.title: Quick note on vectors
docs.text:
Positions, sizes and velocities are stored in vectors. Vector3(x, y, z) is the one you'll use most. Vectors support the math you'd expect:

a = Vector3(1, 0, 0)
b = Vector3(0, 1, 0)

c = a + b          # Vector3(1, 1, 0)
d = a * 5.0        # Vector3(5, 0, 0)

docs.title: 6. Reading keyboard input
docs.text:
Use Input to check which keys the player is pressing:

def Process(self, delta):
    if Input.is_key_pressed(Key.SPACE):
        Console.Print("Space is being held down")

There are three kinds of checks:

Method True when Input.is_key_pressed(key) The key is held down (every frame) Input.is_key_just_pressed(key) The key was pressed this frame Input.is_key_released(key) The key was released this frame

Keys live in the Key module: Key.A–Key.Z, Key.NUM_0–Key.NUM_9, Key.SPACE, Key.ENTER, Key.ESCAPE, Key.LEFT_SHIFT, and the arrows Key.UP, Key.DOWN, Key.LEFT, Key.RIGHT.

Mouse buttons work the same way with Input.is_mouse_button_pressed(Mouse.LEFT) and friends.

docs.title: 7. Building a basic movement system
docs.text:
Let's put it all together and make an object move with WASD.

from fusion import *


class Player(Script):
    def OnStart(self):
        self.transform = self.get_component(TransformComponent)
        self.speed = 5.0

    def Process(self, delta):
        direction = Vector3(0, 0, 0)

        if Input.is_key_pressed(Key.W):
            direction = direction + Vector3(0, 1, 0)
        if Input.is_key_pressed(Key.S):
            direction = direction + Vector3(0, -1, 0)
        if Input.is_key_pressed(Key.A):
            direction = direction + Vector3(-1, 0, 0)
        if Input.is_key_pressed(Key.D):
            direction = direction + Vector3(1, 0, 0)

        self.transform.world_position = (
            self.transform.world_position + direction * self.speed * delta
        )

Press Play and move around with WASD.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Every frame we start with a direction of zero.
  2. Each held key adds a direction to it. Holding W and D together gives you up-and-right.
  3. We multiply the direction by speed to say how fast to move, and by delta so that the speed is measured in units per second. Without delta, your object would move faster on a faster computer.
  4. We add the result to the current position.

docs.title: Fixing diagonal speed
docs.text:
Moving diagonally is currently faster than moving in a straight line, because the direction (1, 1, 0) is longer than (1, 0, 0). Normalizing the direction fixes that:

        if direction != Vector3(0, 0, 0):
            direction = direction.normalized()

Put this just before the line that updates world_position. normalized() returns a new vector with a length of 1, pointing the same way.

Note

Vector3 and Vector4 use normalized(), while Vector2 calls the same thing normalize(). Both return a new vector rather than changing the original.

docs.title: 8. Tweaking values from the inspector
docs.text:
Hard-coding self.speed = 5.0 means you have to edit the script every time you want to try a different speed. Instead, you can export the value so it shows up in the inspector:

from fusion import *


class Player(Script):
    speed = export_drag(5.0, 0.0, 20.0)

    def OnStart(self):
        self.transform = self.get_component(TransformComponent)

    def Process(self, delta):
        # ... same movement code as before, using self.speed
        ...

Exports are written as class-level assignments (outside of any function). The most common ones:

Function Use it for export(value) Any value, with the default widget for its type export_range(value, min, max) A number between a minimum and maximum export_drag(value, min, max) A click-and-drag number field export_color_edit(value) A color export_file(value, "*.png") A file from your project

You can change the value in the inspector while the game is running to find what feels right, which makes tuning movement much faster.

docs.title: 9. Going further: physics-based movement
docs.text:
The movement above directly changes the object's position. If your object has a RigidBodyComponent, you can move it with physics instead, so it collides with and is pushed by other objects.

from fusion import *


class PhysicsPlayer(Script):
    speed = export_drag(5.0, 0.0, 20.0)
    jump_speed = export_drag(8.0, 0.0, 30.0)

    def OnStart(self):
        self.body = self.get_component(RigidBodyComponent)
        self.collision = self.get_component(CollisionComponent)

        Input.on_key_just_pressed(Key.SPACE, self.jump)

    def Process(self, delta):
        move = 0.0
        if Input.is_key_pressed(Key.A):
            move -= 1.0
        if Input.is_key_pressed(Key.D):
            move += 1.0

        # Set horizontal speed, keep the current vertical speed (gravity, jumps)
        current = self.body.velocity
        self.body.velocity = Vector3(move * self.speed, current.y, 0)

    def jump(self):
        if self.collision.is_grounded():
            current = self.body.velocity
            self.body.velocity = Vector3(current.x, self.jump_speed, 0)

Two new ideas here:

  • Callbacks. Input.on_key_just_pressed(Key.SPACE, self.jump) tells the engine to call self.jump whenever Space is pressed, so you don't have to check for it every frame.
  • Grounded check. is_grounded() on the CollisionComponent tells you whether the object is standing on something, so the player can't jump in mid-air.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
Forgetting delta. Movement that isn't multiplied by delta depends on frame rate.

Looking up components in Process. Fetch them once in OnStart and store them on self.

Forgetting self. Inside a class, use self.speed, not speed, when you want to read a value stored on the script.

Nothing happens. Make sure the script is attached to an object, and check the Console for errors.
